vignette:
At 39, she still returns in her mind to the afternoon the earth began to move. Before the disaster, her life is structured around military routine, shared meals with her husband, and the demands of soldiering that have become familiar over the years. She is Latin American, proud of her discipline and endurance, and she has long carried herself as someone who can stay steady when others cannot. That belief is shaken during the natural disaster, when everything she knows about safety and control collapses in minutes.

She describes the moment as if the ground itself turned against her. One instant she is standing with other soldiers, assessing damage and preparing to assist civilians; the next, walls crack, alarms sound, and dust fills the air. She remembers the violent motion of the floor, the sound of concrete giving way, and the unsteady, disorienting sensation that she cannot trust her own body to keep her upright. What stands out most is not only fear but helplessness. In her work she is used to acting quickly, following orders, moving toward danger rather than away from it. During the disaster, there is nowhere to go, nothing to fix, and that loss of agency stays with her.

In the days that follow, she throws herself into rescue efforts. Her military training carries her through long shifts, but she notices she is operating on something close to autopilot. She works because that is what she knows how to do, and because stopping feels impossible. At home, her husband sees that she is tense and distant, but she cannot yet name what is happening inside her. She sleeps lightly, waking at every sound. When aftershocks or loud machinery shake the building, she is flooded with the same panic she felt during the disaster. Her body reacts before her mind catches up: heart racing, muscles braced, breath shallow, eyes scanning for exits.

Over time, the memories begin to intrude in sharper ways. She does not simply remember the earthquake; she relives pieces of it. A rumble in the street, a vibration from a passing truck, or the clatter of dishes can make her feel suddenly back in the collapsing chaos. She starts avoiding places that feel enclosed or unstable. She prefers to sit near doors, checks structural cracks in buildings, and notices ceilings in a way she never did before. At work, she pays close attention to emergency routes and safety procedures, but even these familiar tasks now carry an edge of dread. She pushes through because her role demands it, yet she is more irritable with colleagues and more easily startled by unexpected noises.

At home, she is less patient and more withdrawn. Her husband asks what she needs, and she often says “nothing,” though she is increasingly tense, tired, and on guard. She feels guilty for not being the same woman she was before, and ashamed that a soldier can still be frightened by something she cannot shoot or outrun. She tries to stay busy because quiet moments leave too much room for images of falling debris, dust-covered faces, and the sickening feeling of being trapped. When she does sleep, her dreams are restless. She wakes with her sheets tangled around her legs, sometimes reaching for her phone before fully orienting herself, as if she needs to confirm that the world is still intact.

She also notices a change in her mood. Activities that once gave her satisfaction feel flat. She remains capable and functional on the outside, but inside she feels disconnected, as though part of her stayed under the rubble. She avoids talking about the disaster except in brief, practical terms with others who were there. The more she tries to seal it off, the more present it becomes. Months later, she still measures herself against the version of herself who moved confidently through danger, and she struggles with the sense that she has become weaker in a way that no one else can see.

Even now, she continues to serve, to care for her home, and to meet the expectations of her life with determination. But the disaster remains close to the surface. It lives in the way she startles, the way she scans a room before settling, the way her body tenses when the ground feels uncertain. She moves forward, yet always with part of her listening for the next sound that means everything has begun to break again.
